props.title: Taking Chance

sections.content: Taking Chance represents a pivotal moment in how American cinema portrayed military casualties and the solemn process of returning fallen soldiers home. Unlike bombastic war films like Saving Private Ryan (1998) or Black Hawk Down (2001), this HBO film follows a single Marine casualty's journey with intimate precision. Kevin Bacon delivers a masterfully restrained performance as Lt. Colonel Michael Strobl, escorting the body of PFC Chance Phelps. The film's power lies in its methodical attention to military protocol and the quiet moments of respect shown by ordinary Americans along the route.

sections.content: The film sparked a wave of more nuanced military dramas that focused on the human cost of war rather than combat itself. The Messenger (2009) examined the psychological toll on casualty notification officers, while Brothers (2009) explored how death and trauma reverberate through military families. These films marked a shift from the adrenaline-fueled war narratives of the past to more contemplative examinations of service and sacrifice. SUBHEAD: Military Protocol and Civilian Response

Taking Chance uniquely captures the intersection between military precision and civilian gratitude. Every handler, driver, and airport worker who encounters PFC Phelps's transfer case demonstrates deep respect, creating a portrait of America's relationship with its fallen soldiers. This influenced later films like Last Flag Flying (2017) and Thank You for Your Service (2017), which similarly explored the gap between military and civilian life while honoring fallen service members.
